title: Periodontal Pockets & Bone Loss Patterns — Test

mcqs.q: A periodontal pocket is defined as:
opts: A gingival sulcus lined by oral epithelium
A defect in the alveolar bone only
mcqs.explain: It results from apical migration of the junctional epithelium accompanied by attachment loss.

mcqs.q: Deepening of the gingival sulcus may result from:
opts: Coronal movement of the gingival margin, apical displacement of the attachment, or both
Apical displacement of the attachment only
Coronal movement of the gingival margin only
mcqs.explain: Either process, or a combination of the two, deepens the sulcus.

mcqs.q: A GINGIVAL pocket (pseudopocket) is characterised by:
opts: Gingival enlargement without destruction of the underlying periodontal tissues
Apical migration of the junctional epithelium
mcqs.explain: The sulcus is deepened because of the increased bulk of the gingiva, not because of tissue destruction.

mcqs.q: In a SUPRABONY pocket the base of the pocket is:
opts: Coronal to the underlying alveolar bone
Apical to the crest of the alveolar bone
At the level of the CEJ
mcqs.explain: Suprabony (supracrestal/supraalveolar) pockets are accompanied by horizontal bone loss.

mcqs.q: In an INFRABONY pocket the pattern of bone loss is:
mcqs.explain: The base of an infrabony (intrabony/subcrestal) pocket lies apical to the adjacent bone crest, with the pocket wall between tooth and bone.

mcqs.q: Interproximally, the transseptal fibres in a SUPRABONY pocket are arranged:
mcqs.explain: In infrabony pockets the transseptal fibres are oblique, following the angular pattern of the adjacent bone.

mcqs.q: On facial and lingual surfaces of a SUPRABONY pocket, the periodontal ligament fibres beneath the pocket:
opts: Follow their normal horizontal–oblique course between tooth and bone
Follow the angular pattern of the adjacent bone
Run parallel to the root surface
mcqs.explain: In infrabony pockets they instead follow the angular pattern of the adjacent bone.

mcqs.q: A pocket that originates on one tooth surface and twists around the tooth to involve additional surfaces is termed:
mcqs.explain: Simple involves one surface, compound two, and complex (spiral) more — complex pockets are most common in furcation areas.

mcqs.q: Complex (spiral) pockets are MOST common in:
mcqs.explain: The anatomy of the furcation favours pockets twisting around the roots.

mcqs.q: The initial lesion in the development of periodontitis is:
opts: Inflammation of the gingiva in response to a bacterial challenge
Apical migration of the junctional epithelium
mcqs.explain: Pocket formation starts as an inflammatory change in the connective tissue wall of the gingival sulcus.

mcqs.q: Apical to the junctional epithelium during pocket formation:
opts: Collagen fibres are destroyed and the area is occupied by inflammatory cells and edema
mcqs.explain: The cellular and fluid inflammatory exudate degenerates the surrounding connective tissue including the gingival fibres.

mcqs.q: The junctional epithelium loses cohesiveness and detaches from the tooth when PMNs reach approximately what proportion of its volume?
mcqs.explain: At ~60% PMN volume the tissue loses cohesiveness; the coronal portion detaches while the apical portion migrates, producing the apical shift.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT typically found among the contents of a periodontal pocket?
opts: Microorganisms with their enzymes and endotoxins
mcqs.explain: Contents include microorganisms and their products, gingival fluid, food remnants, salivary mucin, desquamated epithelial cells, leukocytes and plaque-covered calculus.

mcqs.q: Regarding pus in a periodontal pocket, which statement is CORRECT?
opts: It is a secondary sign that does not indicate pocket depth or severity of destruction
Its presence confirms a deep pocket
It correlates directly with the amount of bone loss
It is always absent in periodontitis
mcqs.explain: Pus merely reflects the nature of the inflammatory changes in the pocket wall.

mcqs.q: The observation that periodontal destruction does not occur in all parts of the mouth at the same time is called:
mcqs.explain: Site specificity is a fundamental characteristic of periodontal disease.

mcqs.q: Pulp changes associated with periodontal pockets occur through the:
opts: Apical foramen or lateral pulp canals
Dentinal tubules of the crown only
mcqs.explain: Infection from the pocket reaches the pulp via the apical foramen or lateral canals.

mcqs.q: Which statement about pocket depth and attachment loss is TRUE?
opts: Pockets of the same depth may have different degrees of attachment loss
Pocket depth always equals attachment loss
Deeper pockets always mean more attachment loss
Attachment loss cannot occur without a deep pocket
mcqs.explain: Conversely, pockets of different depths may be associated with the same amount of attachment loss.

mcqs.q: Extensive attachment and bone loss may be associated with SHALLOW pockets when there is:
mcqs.explain: Conversely, slight bone loss can occur with deep pockets if accompanied by gingival enlargement.

mcqs.q: Interproximally, inflammation spreads from the gingiva by which route?
opts: Gingiva → bone → periodontal ligament, and gingiva → periodontal ligament
Via the lymphatics of the tongue
mcqs.explain: Facially and lingually the routes are gingiva → outer periosteum, periosteum → bone, and gingiva → periodontal ligament.

mcqs.q: Facially and lingually, inflammation spreads from the gingiva FIRST along the:
mcqs.explain: From the gingiva along the outer periosteum, then from the periosteum into the bone, and also from the gingiva into the PDL.

mcqs.q: The MOST common pattern of bone loss in periodontal disease is:
mcqs.explain: In horizontal bone loss the bone margin remains approximately perpendicular to the tooth surface.

mcqs.q: In horizontal bone loss, the bone margin:
opts: Remains approximately perpendicular to the tooth surface
Runs obliquely apical to the surrounding bone
Forms a crater between facial and lingual walls
mcqs.explain: The height of bone is reduced but the contour stays roughly level, and it accompanies suprabony pockets.

mcqs.q: Vertical (angular) defects are characterised by:
opts: An oblique direction with the base apical to the surrounding bone
A base coronal to the surrounding bone
A margin perpendicular to the tooth
mcqs.explain: In most instances angular defects have accompanying infrabony periodontal pockets.

mcqs.q: Angular (vertical) bony defects are classified according to:
opts: The number of remaining bony walls — 1, 2 or 3 walled
mcqs.explain: More remaining walls mean a better contained defect, which is more amenable to regeneration.

mcqs.q: An osseous crater is defined as:
opts: A concavity in the crest of interdental bone confined within the facial and lingual walls
A bony enlargement of the alveolar process
Loss of radicular bone with intact interdental bone
mcqs.explain: Craters are concavities of the interdental crest bounded by the facial and lingual plates.

mcqs.q: Ledges are best described as:
opts: Plateau-like bone margins caused by resorption of thickened bony plates
mcqs.explain: Bulbous bone contours are bony enlargements; reversed architecture is loss of interdental bone without loss of radicular bone.

mcqs.q: 'Reversed architecture' refers to:
opts: Loss of interdental bone without a concomitant loss of radicular bone
Loss of radicular bone with intact interdental bone
Bony exostoses on the facial plate
mcqs.explain: It reverses the normal (positive) scalloped architecture of the alveolar bone.

mcqs.q: Furcation involvement is:
opts: Invasion of the bifurcation or trifurcation of multirooted teeth by periodontitis
A defect of single-rooted teeth only
Always associated with horizontal bone loss only
mcqs.explain: Complex spiral pockets are most common in furcation areas, making them hard to clean and treat.

mcqs.q: Suprabony pockets are PRIMARILY treated by:
opts: Resective procedures such as gingivectomy or osseous surgery
mcqs.explain: Infrabony defects with multiple (contained) walls are amenable to regenerative approaches.

mcqs.q: Which defect is MOST amenable to a regenerative approach?
mcqs.explain: The more bony walls remaining, the better contained the defect and the more predictable regeneration becomes.

saqs.q: Define the periodontal pocket and distinguish a gingival pocket from a true periodontal pocket.
saqs.a: A periodontal pocket is a pathologically deepened gingival sulcus, resulting from apical migration of the junctional epithelium accompanied by attachment loss. Deepening may occur by coronal movement of the gingival margin, apical displacement of the gingival attachment, or a combination of the two. A gingival pocket (pseudopocket) is formed by gingival enlargement without destruction of the underlying periodontal tissues — the sulcus is deepened simply because of the increased bulk of the gingiva. A true periodontal pocket, by contrast, produces destruction of the supporting periodontal tissues, leading to loosening and eventual exfoliation of the teeth.

saqs.q: Tabulate the distinguishing features of suprabony and infrabony periodontal pockets.
saqs.a: Base of the pocket — suprabony: coronal to the level of the alveolar bone; infrabony: apical to the crest of the alveolar bone. Pattern of bone loss — suprabony: horizontal; infrabony: vertical (angular). Transseptal fibres interproximally — suprabony: arranged horizontally; infrabony: oblique. Periodontal ligament fibres beneath the pocket on facial and lingual surfaces — suprabony: follow their normal horizontal–oblique course between the tooth and bone; infrabony: follow the angular pattern of the adjacent bone. Clinically, suprabony pockets are treated primarily by resective procedures (gingivectomy, osseous surgery), whereas contained multi-walled infrabony defects are amenable to regeneration.

saqs.q: Describe the pathogenesis of periodontal pocket formation.
saqs.a: The initial lesion is inflammation of the gingiva in response to a bacterial challenge. Pocket formation begins as an inflammatory change in the connective tissue wall of the gingival sulcus. The cellular and fluid inflammatory exudate causes degeneration of the surrounding connective tissue, including the gingival fibres. Apical to the junctional epithelium, collagen fibres are destroyed and the area becomes occupied by inflammatory cells and edema. Polymorphonuclear leukocytes invade the coronal end of the junctional epithelium in increasing numbers; when their relative volume reaches approximately 60% or more of the junctional epithelium, the tissue loses its cohesiveness and detaches from the tooth surface. Thus the coronal portion of the junctional epithelium detaches from the root while the apical portion migrates, producing an apical shift of the attachment and deepening the pocket.

saqs.q: List the contents of a periodontal pocket and state the significance of pus.
saqs.a: Periodontal pockets contain debris consisting principally of microorganisms and their products (enzymes, endotoxins and other metabolic products), together with gingival fluid, food remnants, salivary mucin, desquamated epithelial cells and leukocytes; plaque-covered calculus usually projects from the tooth surface. Pus is a common feature of periodontal disease but it is only a SECONDARY sign: it is not an indication of the depth of the pocket nor of the severity of destruction of the supporting tissues, and merely reflects the nature of the inflammatory changes in the pocket wall.

saqs.q: Explain the relationship between pocket depth, attachment loss and bone loss.
saqs.a: Pockets of the same depth may be associated with different degrees of attachment loss, and pockets of different depths may be associated with the same amount of attachment loss — so probing depth alone is not a measure of destruction. The severity of bone loss is generally, but not always, correlated with pocket depth: extensive attachment and bone loss may be associated with shallow pockets when the attachment loss is accompanied by recession of the gingival margin, and conversely only slight bone loss may occur with deep pockets when these are accompanied by gingival enlargement. Regarding the pocket–bone relationship, in infrabony pockets the base is apical to the alveolar crest with the pocket wall lying between tooth and bone, so bone loss is vertical; in suprabony pockets the base is coronal to the crest with the wall coronal to the bone, so bone loss is always horizontal.

saqs.q: Describe the pathways of spread of inflammation and the patterns of bone destruction in periodontal disease.
saqs.a: Pathways: interproximally, inflammation spreads (1) from the gingiva into the bone, (2) from the bone into the periodontal ligament, and (3) from the gingiva into the periodontal ligament. Facially and lingually it spreads (1) from the gingiva along the outer periosteum, (2) from the periosteum into the bone, and (3) from the gingiva into the periodontal ligament. Patterns of bone destruction: horizontal bone loss — the most common pattern, in which the bone margin remains approximately perpendicular to the tooth surface; vertical or angular defects — occurring in an oblique direction with the base apical to the surrounding bone, usually with accompanying infrabony pockets and classified as 1-, 2- or 3-walled; osseous craters — concavities in the crest of the interdental bone confined within the facial and lingual walls; bulbous bone contours — bony enlargements; ledges — plateau-like bone margins caused by resorption of thickened bony plates; reversed architecture — loss of interdental bone without a concomitant loss of radicular bone; and furcation involvement — invasion of the bifurcation or trifurcation of multirooted teeth.
